chapter.title: Design a Rate Limiter
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.goal: Design a scalable distributed API rate limiter and understand its algorithms, architecture, failure modes, client behavior, and operational tradeoffs.

summary.definition: A rate limiter controls the rate of traffic sent by a client or service. In HTTP systems it limits the number of client requests permitted over a specified period; excess calls are blocked.
benefits: Prevent resource starvation caused by intentional or unintentional DoS behavior.
Reduce cost by limiting excess calls and preserving resources for high-priority APIs.
Reduce paid third-party API usage when providers charge per call.
Prevent server overload caused by bots or user misbehavior.
examples: No more than 2 posts per second per user.
No more than 10 account creations per day from the same IP.
No more than 5 reward claims per week from the same device.

requirements.name: Low latency
requirements.detail: The limiter should not noticeably slow HTTP response time.

requirements.name: Memory efficiency
requirements.detail: Use as little memory as possible.

requirements.name: Distributed rate limiting
requirements.detail: The limiter must be shareable across multiple servers or processes.

requirements.name: Exception handling
requirements.detail: Show clear exceptions to users when requests are throttled.

requirements.name: High fault tolerance
requirements.detail: Problems in the limiter, such as cache-server failure, should not take down the whole system.

scope_clarification.question: Throttle by IP, user ID, or other properties?
scope_clarification.answer: Support flexible sets of throttle rules.

scope_clarification.question: What scale?
scope_clarification.answer: Handle a large number of requests.

reasons: Requests can be forged by malicious actors.
The service may not control client implementation.

server_side.description: Rate limiting can be implemented within the server-side API infrastructure.

middleware.description: A rate-limiter middleware can sit between clients and API servers.
middleware.example: If the API permits 2 requests/second and the client sends 3, the first 2 pass and the third gets HTTP 429.

api_gateway.description: A managed middleware component that may support rate limiting, SSL termination, authentication, IP whitelisting, static content, and other functions.

decision_guidelines: Evaluate the existing technology stack and cache service.
Choose an algorithm that fits business needs.
Server-side implementation provides more algorithm control; third-party gateways may limit options.
If an API gateway already exists for authentication or IP whitelisting, rate limiting can be added there.
If engineering resources are limited, a commercial API gateway may be preferable.

algorithms.name: Token Bucket
mechanism: A bucket has a predefined token capacity.
Tokens are added periodically at a preset refill rate.
Extra refill tokens overflow when the bucket is full.
If enough tokens exist, the request passes.
If not, the request is dropped.

parameters.bucket_size: Maximum number of tokens in the bucket.
parameters.refill_rate: Number of tokens added per unit time.

bucket_examples: Different API endpoints may require different buckets.
Rate limiting by IP can require one bucket per IP.
A global request ceiling can use one shared global bucket.
pros: Allows short bursts while tokens remain.
cons: Bucket size and refill rate can be difficult to tune.

algorithms.name: Leaking Bucket
mechanism: Usually implemented with a FIFO queue.
If the queue is not full, the arriving request is added.
If the queue is full, the request is dropped.
Requests are pulled and processed at regular intervals.

parameters.outflow_rate: How many requests are processed at a fixed rate.

pros: Memory efficient because queue size is bounded.
Suitable when a stable output rate is required.
cons: Burst traffic can fill the queue with old requests and cause recent requests to be rate limited.
Queue size and outflow rate can be difficult to tune.

algorithms.name: Fixed Window Counter
mechanism: Divide the timeline into fixed-size windows.
Assign a counter to each window.
Increment the counter for every request.
After the threshold is reached, reject additional requests until the next window.
algorithms.boundary_problem: Traffic near the boundary between adjacent windows can exceed the intended quota within a rolling interval.
algorithms.chapter_example: With a 5-requests/minute limit, 5 requests near the end of one minute plus 5 just after the next minute begins can yield 10 requests between 2:00:30 and 2:01:30.
pros: Window resets fit some use cases.
cons: Boundary spikes can allow more requests than intended.

algorithms.name: Sliding Window Log
mechanism: Store request timestamps, typically in cache such as Redis sorted sets.
Remove timestamps older than the beginning of the current rolling window.
If the log size is within the allowed count, accept; otherwise reject.
chapter_example: 1:00:50 rejected because log size becomes 3; timestamp may still remain.
1:01:40 removes timestamps before 1:00:40, then accepts the request.
pros: Very accurate; requests do not exceed the rate in a rolling window.
cons: Uses more memory because timestamps, including rejected-request timestamps, can remain stored.

algorithms.name: Sliding Window Counter
algorithms.mechanism: Hybrid of fixed window counter and sliding window log. Estimate the rolling-window count as current-window requests plus a weighted portion of the previous window.
algorithms.formula: current requests + previous requests * overlap percentage

chapter_example.source_note: The text prints '0.7%' while the figure shows 70% and the stated result is 6.5. This guide preserves the source discrepancy.
chapter_example.result: 6.5, rounded down to 6; request passes because limit is 7.

cons: Approximate because it assumes previous-window requests are evenly distributed.

algorithm_comparison.main_issue: Old queued burst traffic can crowd out new requests

high_level_architecture.counter_principle: Track requests for the relevant user, IP, or other throttle key. If the count is above the limit, disallow the request.

storage_choice.why_not_database: The chapter says database disk access is too slow for this path.

redis_commands.purpose: Set a timeout so the counter is automatically deleted.

flow: Client sends request to rate-limiter middleware.
Middleware reads the corresponding counter from Redis.
Middleware checks whether the limit has been reached.
If not reached, forward to API servers.
Increment the counter and save it in Redis.

rules_and_responses.rule_storage: Rules are generally written in configuration files and stored on disk.
over_limit_behavior: Depending on the use case, drop the request.
Depending on the use case, enqueue the request for later processing.

headers.meaning: Remaining requests allowed within the current window.
Maximum calls allowed per time window.
Seconds to wait before retrying without being throttled.

flow: Workers frequently pull the rules and place them in cache.
Client request reaches rate-limiter middleware first.
Middleware fetches counters and the last request timestamp from Redis.
If allowed, forward to API servers.
If blocked, return 429 and either drop or queue the request.

race_condition.problem: Concurrent requests can read the same Redis counter before either writes an update, producing a lost increment.
race_condition.chapter_example: Counter starts at 3. Two requests both read 3 and each writes 4; logically it should become 5.

synchronization.problem: The same client can reach different rate-limiter instances, so isolated local state is insufficient.
synchronization.not_recommended: Sticky sessions; the chapter calls them neither scalable nor flexible.
synchronization.preferred: Centralized shared state such as Redis.

performance.reason: Users far from a data center experience higher latency.
performance.approach: Route traffic to geographically close edge servers.

examples: If rules are too strict and valid requests are dropped, relax the rules.
If flash-sale bursts make the limiter ineffective, consider changing algorithms; the chapter says token bucket is a good fit.

additional_talking_points.hard_rate_limiting: The number of requests cannot exceed the threshold.
additional_talking_points.soft_rate_limiting: Requests may exceed the threshold for a short period.

layers.main_chapter_focus: Application-level HTTP rate limiting, OSI layer 7.
layers.other_example: IP-based rate limiting with Iptables at OSI layer 3.

client_best_practices: Use client caching to avoid unnecessary API calls.
Understand the limit and avoid sending too many requests in a short interval.
Add sufficient backoff time to retry logic.

flashcards.front: What does a rate limiter do?
flashcards.back: Controls how many requests a client or service may send over a specified period.

flashcards.front: What are the three main benefits discussed?
flashcards.back: Prevent resource starvation/DoS effects, reduce cost, and prevent server overload.

flashcards.front: What kind of limiter is designed?
flashcards.back: A server-side API rate limiter.

flashcards.front: What are the six requirements?
flashcards.back: Accurate limiting, low latency, low memory use, distributed operation, clear exception handling, and high fault tolerance.

flashcards.front: Why is client-side enforcement unreliable?
flashcards.back: Requests can be forged and the service may not control client implementation.

flashcards.front: What status code means too many requests?
flashcards.back: HTTP 429.

flashcards.front: What is an API gateway in this chapter?
flashcards.back: Middleware that may provide rate limiting plus SSL termination, authentication, IP whitelisting, static content, and related functions.

flashcards.front: Name all five rate-limiting algorithms.
flashcards.back: Token bucket, leaking bucket, fixed window counter, sliding window log, sliding window counter.

flashcards.front: How does token bucket work?
flashcards.back: Requests consume replenished tokens; if a token exists the request passes, otherwise it is dropped.

flashcards.front: What are token bucket's two parameters?
flashcards.back: Bucket size and refill rate.

flashcards.front: What is token bucket's major burst advantage?
flashcards.back: It allows short bursts while tokens remain.

flashcards.front: What is token bucket's main downside?
flashcards.back: Bucket size and refill rate can be hard to tune.

flashcards.front: How is leaking bucket usually implemented?
flashcards.back: As a FIFO queue processed at a fixed outflow rate.

flashcards.front: What happens when the leaking-bucket queue is full?
flashcards.back: The arriving request is dropped.

flashcards.front: When is leaking bucket suitable?
flashcards.back: When a stable outflow rate is required.

flashcards.front: How does fixed window counter work?
flashcards.back: It counts requests in fixed time windows and blocks new requests after the threshold until the next window.

flashcards.front: What is the fixed-window boundary problem?
flashcards.back: Requests clustered around adjacent window boundaries can exceed the intended rolling quota.

flashcards.front: What does sliding window log store?
flashcards.back: Individual request timestamps.

flashcards.front: What is the main strength of sliding window log?
flashcards.back: Very accurate rolling-window enforcement.

flashcards.front: What is its main weakness?
flashcards.back: High memory use because timestamps can remain stored, including rejected-request timestamps.

flashcards.front: What does sliding window counter combine?
flashcards.back: Fixed window counter and sliding window log.

flashcards.front: Why is sliding window counter approximate?
flashcards.back: It assumes previous-window requests were evenly distributed.

flashcards.front: Why does the architecture choose Redis?
flashcards.back: It is an in-memory store that is fast and supports expiration.

flashcards.front: What does Redis INCR do?
flashcards.back: Increments a stored counter by one.

flashcards.front: What does Redis EXPIRE do?
flashcards.back: Sets a timeout so a counter is automatically deleted.

flashcards.front: Where are rate-limit rules generally stored?
flashcards.back: In configuration files saved on disk.

flashcards.front: What does X-Ratelimit-Remaining mean?
flashcards.back: Remaining allowed requests in the window.

flashcards.front: What does X-Ratelimit-Limit mean?
flashcards.back: Maximum calls allowed per time window.

flashcards.front: What does X-Ratelimit-Retry-After mean?
flashcards.back: Seconds to wait before retrying without being throttled.

flashcards.front: What can happen to a blocked request besides being dropped?
flashcards.back: It can be queued for later processing when the use case allows it.

flashcards.front: What are the two distributed challenges?
flashcards.back: Race condition and synchronization.

flashcards.front: What is the race-condition example?
flashcards.back: Two requests both read counter 3 and each writes 4, even though the logical result should be 5.

flashcards.front: Why not solve the race condition only with locks?
flashcards.back: The chapter says locks significantly slow the system.

flashcards.front: What alternatives are referenced?
flashcards.back: Lua scripts and Redis sorted sets.

flashcards.front: Why are sticky sessions not preferred?
flashcards.back: They are neither scalable nor flexible.

flashcards.front: What synchronization approach is preferred?
flashcards.back: Centralized shared state such as Redis.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple data centers or edge locations?
flashcards.back: To reduce latency for geographically distant users.

flashcards.front: What consistency model is suggested?
flashcards.back: Eventual consistency.

flashcards.front: What should monitoring verify?
flashcards.back: That both the algorithm and the rules are effective.

flashcards.front: Which algorithm is identified as good for burst traffic?
flashcards.back: Token bucket.

flashcards.front: What is hard rate limiting?
flashcards.back: Requests cannot exceed the threshold.

flashcards.front: What is soft rate limiting?
flashcards.back: Requests may exceed the threshold briefly.

flashcards.front: What OSI layer is HTTP rate limiting?
flashcards.back: Layer 7, application layer.

flashcards.front: Name four client best practices.
flashcards.back: Cache, understand limits, catch errors, and use sufficient retry backoff.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can rate limiting reduce cost?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: By blocking excess requests, the system may need fewer resources and can avoid unnecessary paid third-party API calls.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is the rate limiter placed server-side or in middleware rather than trusted solely to the client?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Clients can be forged and the service may not control client implementation, so trusted enforcement must occur in service-controlled infrastructure.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare token bucket and leaking bucket.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Token bucket consumes replenished tokens and permits short bursts while tokens remain. Leaking bucket queues requests and releases them at a fixed rate, which produces stable outflow but can cause newer requests to be rejected when a burst fills the queue.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the fixed-window boundary problem.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Each fixed window may independently remain under quota even though a rolling interval spanning the boundary contains far more requests than intended.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare sliding window log and sliding window counter.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Sliding log stores individual timestamps and is accurate but memory intensive. Sliding counter weights previous-window traffic, making it memory efficient but approximate.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is Redis used?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The limiter requires fast hot-path state updates. Redis is in memory and provides INCR and EXPIRE for counters and time windows.

short_answer_questions.question: How are rate-limit rules distributed?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Rules are stored on disk, workers frequently pull them into a cache, and rate-limiter middleware reads them from the cache.

short_answer_questions.question: What distributed problems must be handled?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Race conditions during concurrent updates and synchronization across multiple rate-limiter instances.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is centralized Redis better than sticky sessions in the chapter's synchronization design?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Sticky sessions are described as neither scalable nor flexible, while shared Redis gives all limiter instances access to common state.

short_answer_questions.question: What should production monitoring tell you?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Whether the algorithm works effectively for real traffic and whether the configured rules are appropriately strict or need adjustment.

common_confusions.correction: The chapter calls client-side enforcement unreliable because requests can be forged and client code may be uncontrolled.

common_confusions.confusion: The API gateway is always the correct placement.
common_confusions.correction: There is no absolute answer; placement depends on stack, control needs, resources, and existing architecture.

common_confusions.confusion: Token bucket and leaking bucket handle bursts the same way.
common_confusions.correction: Token bucket allows bursts while tokens remain; leaking bucket queues and drains requests at a fixed rate.

common_confusions.confusion: Fixed window gives exact rolling-window enforcement.
common_confusions.correction: Boundary spikes can exceed the intended rolling quota.

common_confusions.confusion: Sliding window log is memory efficient.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter identifies memory consumption as its primary downside.
It is approximate because it assumes previous-window requests are evenly distributed.

common_confusions.confusion: The printed sliding-counter example is internally consistent.
common_confusions.correction: The source text prints '0.7%' while the figure shows 70% and the stated result is 6.5; this guide preserves that discrepancy.

common_confusions.confusion: Sticky sessions are the best distributed synchronization solution.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter says they are neither scalable nor flexible and prefers centralized Redis.

must_memorize: Requirements: accuracy, low latency, low memory, distributed support, exception handling, fault tolerance.
Algorithms: token bucket, leaking bucket, fixed window, sliding log, sliding counter.
Fixed window = simple but boundary spike risk.
Redis INCR increments; EXPIRE sets timeout.
Rules live on disk and are cached.
Distributed issues: race condition and synchronization.

final_review.memory_chain: Client -> Rate Limiter Middleware -> cached rules + Redis state -> API server if allowed OR HTTP 429/drop/queue if blocked.
final_review.algorithm_memory_chain: TOKEN=burst; LEAK=fixed outflow; FIXED=boundary issue; LOG=accurate/memory-heavy; SLIDING COUNTER=efficient/approximate.
final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: A scalable rate limiter combines an appropriate algorithm with fast shared state, flexible rules, explicit client feedback, distributed concurrency handling, geographic optimization, and monitoring.
